quote: I don't understand why you can't just give me a general idea of what what we're talking about rather than wasting a lot of time.
stewart_read: This is a cost/time objection wrapped in impatience — the schema's flip point ('what's expensive is not switching', reframe using his own $700 bill) was available and unused; rep instead defended methodology.
alternative_hypothesis: Rep may have judged that explaining the no-ballpark policy was necessary procedure, not an objection to flip — but the customer's own words ('wasting a lot of time') mark this as a stall, not a neutral question.
coaching_implication: Coach the flip: 'The $700 bill last month is exactly why we need the real numbers — a generic range could actually undersell your savings.'

quote: I feel like I'm getting a runaround right now... for another reason.
stewart_read: Customer voices a legitimacy/trust suspicion mid-process; rep does not name it directly or reassure on trust, just continues explaining the data requirement.
alternative_hypothesis: Rep could be reading this as pure impatience rather than a trust breach, which is plausible given the wording is about time-wasting, not scam fear.
coaching_implication: A direct reassurance line ('I know this can feel like a runaround — I promise it's just how we build accurate designs, not a stall tactic') would have named the suspicion instead of talking past it.

quote: You're still not answering my question. Just evading everything I want to know about what what's the cost of installation?
stewart_read: Third occurrence of the same cost-ballpark objection; the canonical rebuttal (redirect_to_design, fair-to-ask framing) exists in the schema and was never deployed verbatim or in spirit.
alternative_hypothesis: Rep may have felt the verbal bill read-back in progress was itself the redirect, but the customer's frustration shows he didn't experience it as resolution.
coaching_implication: Use the schema's 'totally fair to ask' redirect early and explicitly rather than only implicitly completing the ask by finishing bill collection.

quote: Okay. Well, don't you need to look at the house and see what kind of sunlight it gets? There's a lot of trees around.
stewart_read: Customer volunteering shading/tree detail is useful design info and mild engagement signal — he's thinking about his specific roof, not just resisting.
coaching_implication: Rep handled this fine (explained satellite + sun study) but could have flagged it forward to the specialist appointment brief as a shading consideration.

quote: I currently have a solar panel on the roof, but it only it it's only for hot water, not for electricity.
stewart_read: Customer discloses an existing solar thermal system on the roof — relevant to roof space/design and to the orphaned_flow logic — rep just logs it ('putting that in my notes') without probing size, placement, or condition.
alternative_hypothesis: This isn't a PV system so orphaned_flow DQ logic doesn't strictly apply, but the roof-space implication for a new PV design still warranted a follow-up question.
coaching_implication: Ask a quick follow-up: 'Where's that panel located on the roof, and how big is it?' to feed the design team.

quote: Last month, the last bill I got was $700.
stewart_read: Strong bill anchor captured cleanly, but rep's reaction ('Woah. Okay.') acknowledges without emotionally flipping it into alignment-against-the-utility.
coaching_implication: Should have flipped immediately: '$700 in one month — that's exactly the kind of bill this program is built to replace.'

quote: Correct. Yeah. You won't be paying them anymore because they charge a lot.
stewart_read: Rep gets pulled into explaining production offset and net metering mechanics in depth — classic closer-tier financial/technical explanation rather than redirecting to the specialist.
alternative_hypothesis: Some minimal reassurance may be needed to keep the customer on the phone, but the length and technical depth (net metering banking explanation) crosses into scope creep.
coaching_implication: Use the escape hatch: 'That's exactly what our specialist walks through in detail — I want to make sure you get the full picture from someone who lives in that data every day.'
